A November evening. Nora has recovered and is sitting with Mrs Pop in the living room. On the table there is an old box of black-and-white photos. Mrs Pop takes one and shows it to Nora.
Look, Nora. This little girl with pigtails is me. I was seven.
How sweet you were! Where was the photo taken?
In my grandparents’ village, near Bistrița. That’s where I spent all my summers.
And what was life like in the village?
Simple, but beautiful. Grandpa had two cows and a horse. Grandma baked bread in the oven every Saturday. The whole house smelled of warm bread.
A television? No, my dear! In those days nobody in the village had a television. We only had an old radio. In the evening we listened to folk music and the news.
And what did you do all day?
In the morning I helped Grandma: I fetched water from the well and fed the hens. In the afternoon we played with the other children in the yard or went to the river.
It sounds like a dream. In Sweden, at my grandparents’, it was similar. They had a red house by a lake, and in summer we swam every day.
You see? Childhood is the same everywhere. Only the language is different.
And this boy behind you, with the big hat?
Ah… That’s Vasile. He was nine and he was our neighbour. He was always pulling my pigtails. Back then I didn’t know I would marry him.

The imperfect endings “-eam”, “-eai”, “-ea” are pronounced with “ea” in one syllable: “a-veam”, “mer-geam”, “fă-ceai”.
In the imperfect, the stress falls on the ending: a-VEAM, lu-CRAM, mer-GEAM. In the compound perfect, on the participle: am a-VUT.
A “ț” in the middle of a word is pronounced clearly: “co-di-țe”, like “ts”.
Two “â”s in the same word: “fân-tâ-nă”. Both are pronounced like “î”.
1. The imperfect: when to use it

The imperfect is the second important past tense. You use it for: (1) habits and repeated actions in the past, (2) descriptions (what someone or something was like), (3) actions that were in progress when something else happened.
Every summer we went to our grandparents. (habit)
The house was small and white. (description)
I was reading when the phone rang. (action in progress)
Think of the imperfect as the “background” of a story, and the compound perfect as its “events”. You will compare them in chapter 14.
Good news: the imperfect is very regular. It is formed from the verb stem + the endings -am / -eam.
-a verbs take -am (lucram, cântam). -ea and -e verbs and most -i verbs take -eam (aveam, mergeam, vorbeam). -î verbs take -am (coboram).
Just as with “sunt / sunt”, “eu” and “noi” have the same form: “eu lucram”, “noi lucram”. The context shows the person.
3. The verbs “a fi”, “a avea” and other special forms
Other useful forms: a da → dădeam, a sta → stăteam, a bea → beam, a vrea → voiam (or vroiam in speech), a ști → știam, a lua → luam.
I would sit at the window for hours.
4. Expressions for the past and habits

Children’s stories begin with “A fost odată ca niciodată…” (Once upon a time…). Then they continue in the imperfect: “…era un împărat care avea trei fete.” (…there was an emperor who had three daughters.)
A good memory combines a description of the place, the people and the habits:
My grandparents lived in a small village.
Their house had a big yard with an old walnut tree.
Grandpa was tall and didn’t talk much.
Grandma was always in the kitchen.
In the evening we all sat on the bench in front of the house.

I, Mițu, know every corner of this flat. But there is one place I didn’t know: the box on top of the wardrobe in Mrs Pop’s bedroom. It’s too high. Even for an athletic tomcat like me.
Last night the box finally came down onto the living-room table. And I learned that Mrs Pop hasn’t always been old.

Long ago, Mrs Pop was a skinny little girl with pigtails and scraped knees. She was never still. She climbed trees, chased geese and stole cherries from the neighbours’ garden. “I was a little devil,” she said, and Nora laughed.

In another photo, Mrs Pop was eighteen and wore a white dress and a crown of flowers in her hair. She was at her school-leaving ball. “All the boys wanted to dance with me,” she said. “But I danced with only one.”

“With Vasile. We had known each other since we were little. He lived in the house next to my grandparents. Every summer he pulled my pigtails, and I threw apples at his head. We quarrelled all day. And in the evening we both sat on the fence between the yards and looked at the stars.”
Mrs Pop took out a small photo with bent corners. A young man with a moustache and a fluier in his hand was standing on a rock. Behind him you could see the mountains.
“This is from the Turda Gorge,” she said quietly. “I was twenty-four. It was our first trip together. He played the fluier, and I thought it was the most beautiful sound in the world.”
Nora looked at the photo for a long time. Then she took out her phone and showed Mrs Pop the photo from last week: Radu on a rock, with his violin, with the same mountains behind him.
Mrs Pop put the two photos side by side. The same rock. The same angle. Fifty years between them.

Nobody said anything for a long time. I jumped onto the table, slowly, so as not to spoil anything, and I looked too. Vasile looked like Radu. He had the same forehead, the same eyes and the same crooked smile.
“Some things never change,” whispered Mrs Pop. Then she closed the box, but left the two photos on the table, side by side, all night.
In the morning, when I woke up, the photos were still there. And next to them was a small vase with a white rose.

I don’t know who put the rose there. Mrs Pop always wakes up first, at five. Nora sleeps until seven. And I, to be honest, slept all night. But an intelligent tomcat notices one thing: the white rose on Nora’s shelf was no longer on the shelf.
